summary: Kole Jain spends a week learning what gamification is, studies Duolingo as a case study, and then designs a gamified savings app called Fin Base in Figma. He names the key traits he found: gamification is more common than expected, it usually hinges on one central currency, it shows what you have done and what is left, it often has a social side such as leaderboards and badges, and its rewards only work when tied to real goals. His app turns saving into a game: users set goals, earn a currency called fin bits for putting money aside and completing goals, keep a streak, and climb a local leaderboard with promotion and demotion ranges. The onboarding shows the app's value (insights into past spending) before any gamification, and the product ends up as four tabs: goals, leaderboard, analytics and education. For a design system, it is a worked example of a retention pattern set (currency, streaks, leagues, badges, quizzes) rather than of visual tokens.
key_ideas: Gamification is more common than it seems: LinkedIn turns profile completion into an achievement hunt and credit card points are gamified.
Most gamification is built around one central currency (Duolingo XP, Todoist Karma) that shows progress and unlocks features.
Good gamification makes visible what you have accomplished and what is still left, as Exercism does for a coding language.
A social layer, such as leaderboards and public badges, lets people see how they stack up against friends.
Rewards only motivate when they are tied to real goals; a meaningless reward is ignored.
Duolingo layers XP (ranks you, unlocks quest chests), gems (a second currency for modifiers), hearts (lost on wrong answers), streaks and achievements.
The creator skipped task managers and learning platforms because other companies had already gamified them very well, and chose money management instead.
Show the app's value (insights into past spending) in onboarding before you start gamifying.
Scale the reward to the size of the goal, so bigger goals earn more currency.
In the money app, people are ranked on a local leaderboard to account for currency and income differences.
A league leaderboard can have a promotion range, a neutral middle, and a demotion range below.
An education section with quizzes that pay out the currency links learning back to the leaderboard.
Challenges would be nice, but an education section on financial literacy was judged more important.
Designing took far longer than planned: the four main screens took three whole days instead of four to six hours, partly because files kept getting deleted or misplaced.

topics.name: Retention and gamification
topics.summary: Lists the traits of gamification (central currency, visible progress, social comparison, meaningful rewards), breaks down Duolingo's system, and designs a savings app with currency, streaks, goals, badges and leagues.

topics.name: Onboarding
topics.summary: Onboarding welcomes the user, asks them to connect a bank account with reassurance, shows swipeable insights into past spending to prove value before gamifying, then asks for a savings goal with a slider for the time period.

topics.name: Mobile app patterns

topics.name: Dashboards and data display

topics.name: Dark mode and themes

topics.name: Design process

rules.rule: Build the gamification around one central currency (like XP, Karma or fin bits) that is earned by the core actions and shows progress.
rules.why: Most gamification hinges on a central currency; it gives a sense of progress and unlocks features that keep people going.
rules.evidence: most gamification hinges on a Central currency

rules.rule: Show people both what they have accomplished and how much is left, such as the share of a course or goal completed.
rules.why: Gamification gives visibility over progress; Exercism shows exactly how much of a language you have completed and how much is left.
rules.evidence: gamification gives you visibility over what you've accomplished and what's still left

rules.rule: Consider a social layer, such as leaderboards and public badges, so people can compare themselves with friends.
rules.why: Gamification often comes with a social aspect that lets you see how you stack up against your friends.
rules.evidence: leaderboards and public badges are the perfect example

rules.rule: Tie rewards to the user's real goals so they mean something; do not hand out meaningless rewards.
rules.why: Rewards matter, but no one cares if the reward is meaningless.
rules.evidence: no one cares if the reward is meaningless apps tie the rewards to real goals

rules.rule: In onboarding, show the app's value first (for example a swipeable breakdown of past spending and average monthly spend) before introducing any gamification.
rules.why: The source gives no further reason; the creator says to show the value of the app with a few key insights before gamifying.
rules.evidence: before we start gamifying let's show them the value of the app

rules.rule: When onboarding asks for a sensitive connection such as a bank account, add a screen or message that reassures the user their money is safe.
rules.why: The onboarding prompts users to connect their bank and reassures them the app won't steal their money.
rules.evidence: reassuring them we won't steal their money

rules.rule: Scale the reward for completing a goal to the size of the goal.
rules.why: In the example app, completing goals earns fin bits with the amount depending on the size of the goal.
rules.evidence: the amount depending on the size of the goal

rules.rule: When a leaderboard ranks money-related activity, rank people locally rather than globally.
rules.why: A local leaderboard accounts for currency and income differences.
rules.evidence: local leaderboard to account for currency and income differences

rules.rule: Consider a league leaderboard with a promotion range at the top, a neutral middle band, and a demotion range at the bottom.
rules.why: The example app copies Duolingo: above the range you move up a league, in the lower section nothing happens, below it you drop back.
rules.evidence: it uh has a promotion range

rules.rule: Link learning content to the reward loop, for example a quiz at the end of a lesson that pays out the central currency.
rules.why: Taking a quiz earns fin bits, which moves the user up the leaderboard.
rules.evidence: taking a quick quiz at the end will make you earn fin bits

rules.rule: Consider a streak that the core action keeps alive, such as at least one lesson per day on Duolingo, or each time money is put aside in the example app.
rules.why: On Duolingo, doing at least one lesson per day keeps your streak alive; in the example app, putting money aside earns fin bits and continues the streak.
values: at least one lesson per day
rules.evidence: by doing at least one lesson per day you keep your streak alive

rules.rule: Add small perks such as badges or achievements for milestones, for example a badge for saving 30 days in a row.
rules.why: The creator plans badges as small perks; Duolingo gives achievements on milestones along with a gift of gems.
rules.evidence: different badges like one for saving 30 days in a row

rules.rule: When people hold a single real savings account, let them split it into virtual accounts, one per goal.
rules.why: Most people have one savings account, so virtual accounts let them allocate the total amount to various goals.
rules.evidence: we need to make virtual accounts

rules.rule: In a money app, give spending and saving analytics their own tab, with toggles for saving or spending and for daily, weekly or monthly views.
rules.why: The creator says analytics about spending and savings play a critical role.
rules.evidence: you can choose between saving and spending and then daily weekly or monthly

rules.rule: Show insights on when upcoming bill payments are due.
rules.why: So users can prepare for those payments.
rules.evidence: insights as to when new bill payments are going to come up

rules.rule: When onboarding asks for a savings goal, ask whether any amount is already saved and give a slider to set the time period for the goal.
rules.why: The slider lets users adjust the period of time they give themselves to complete the goal.
rules.evidence: a slider to adjust the period of time

decisions.question: What should the gamified app's central currency do?

options.name: Rank only (like Duolingo XP)
options.effect: It cannot buy anything but raises leaderboard rank and unlocks rewards such as quest chests.
options.when: When the currency should measure effort and drive social comparison.

options.name: A second, spendable currency (like Duolingo gems)
options.effect: It buys modifiers such as extra time or more hearts.
options.when: When you want rewards people can spend alongside the ranking currency.

decisions.recommendation: The source makes no general recommendation; the example app uses one currency (fin bits), earned by saving, completing goals and quizzes, and used for leaderboard rank.
decisions.evidence: you can't buy anything with XP

decisions.question: How should the leaderboard group people?

options.name: Global leaderboard
options.when: Not discussed in the source; the creator ranks money-related activity locally instead [inferred].

options.name: Local leaderboard
options.effect: People are ranked within a local group, which accounts for currency and income differences.
options.when: Money-related apps, to account for currency and income differences.

options.name: Leagues with promotion and demotion
options.effect: Top of the board moves up a league, the middle stays, the bottom drops back to a lower league (Stone League in the example).
options.when: When you want a repeating competitive loop like Duolingo's.

decisions.recommendation: The example app ranks locally and adds Duolingo-style leagues with a promotion range.
decisions.evidence: local leaderboard to account for currency and income differences

options.name: Light
options.effect: The first day's onboarding screens, made before the switch to dark mode, so presumably light [inferred].

options.name: Dark

decisions.question: What should onboarding show before asking for a goal?

options.name: Go straight to gamification
options.effect: Users meet goals, streaks and currency before seeing any benefit.
options.when: Not discussed in the source; the creator chose to show value first.

options.name: Show value first
options.effect: Users swipe through insights into their past spending (where they spend, average per month) before setting a goal.
options.when: When the app needs trust and data (such as a bank connection) before the game starts [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: Show the value of the app with a few key insights before gamifying.
decisions.evidence: before we start gamifying let's show them the value of the app

decisions.question: Beside the core game loop, which extra feature should come first: challenges or an education section?

options.name: Challenges
options.effect: On Duolingo, challenges are one of the two activities and earn XP, like lessons.
options.when: The creator calls them cool to incorporate but less important here.

options.name: Education section
options.effect: Lessons on financial literacy (saving, investing, getting a mortgage), with a quick quiz at the end that pays out fin bits.
options.when: When learning supports the goal the app is built around, as in the money app.

decisions.recommendation: The creator says an education section is probably more important than challenges; the final app's four tabs include education and no challenges tab.
decisions.evidence: probably more importantly would be an education section

process.detail: Research examples across apps (LinkedIn, credit card points, Todoist, Exercism, fitness apps) and distil the key traits.
Break down a well-gamified app (Duolingo) into its activities, currencies, rewards, punishments, streaks and achievements, and check it against the traits.
Skip domains already gamified very well (task managers, learning platforms) and choose one that is not (money management).

Define how data comes in (bank connection), what users set (goals), what earns the currency (saving, completing goals), what the currency does (local leaderboard), plus streaks, virtual accounts, analytics, an education section and badges.
Welcome the user, ask them to connect their bank with reassurance, show swipeable spending insights, then ask for a savings goal (and any amount already saved) with a slider for the time period.

process.step: Pick a palette from a reference
process.detail: Take inspiration from an existing palette (Wise) and add a color of your own (purple).
Look at the design again the next day and make bigger changes if needed (here, switching to dark mode).
Build the core screens: goal overview, leaderboard, spending and saving analytics, and education.

caveats: The video description promotes the creator's free Figma files and his design community (13k designers); these are self-promotion and excluded from rules.
This is one designer's week-long experiment on a concept app, not a tested product; no user research or results are shown.
The 'five key things' are not clearly numbered in the transcript; the list here is read from the order he talks through them.
The switch to dark mode and the Wise-inspired palette are shown but not explained, so they are taste, not rules.
Much of the visual design happens in timelapses, so exact colors, type and spacing are not stated.

Auto-caption errors corrected: 'dual lingo' and 'dualingo' read as Duolingo, 'exorcism' as Exercism, 'todoist' as Todoist, 'fin base' as Fin Base, and 'the wise color palette' as the Wise brand's palette [inferred]. The phrase 'fitness apps stas' is unclear and was not guessed.
Jokes about breaking EU privacy laws with bank data are humour; the video does not address privacy or security design.
The video does not discuss the risks of gamification, such as guilt-tripping, beyond joking about Duolingo's 'intense' mascot and incessant reminders.
